ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Participants were instructed to use headphones, set a comfortable listening volume, and listen in a quiet environment.

> Participants were recruited by convenience sampling through university networks and social media, yielding 16, 18, and 34 completed sessions for the three versions (total N = 68 sessions from 65 participants).

> The 13 baseline-only trials (1.6%) were spread across 8 sessions, and no participant gave baseline-only responses throughout a session (maximum 3 of 12 excerpts; individual means ≥ 1.21; peak ratings of 3-5), which suggests that low ratings reflected stimulus-specific neutrality rather than inattention.

> Although participants were instructed to use headphones, we could not control the listening environment, the headphones used (whose frequency response differs between models), or the playback level, which adds unmodeled auditory variance.

Ethics approval statement:

> This study was conducted in accordance with the guidelines of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Ethics Committee of Universidad de Sevilla (Protocol code: SICEIA 2025-0156/ Date of approval: 25/06/2025).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p < 0.05", "p ≥ 0.212", "p < 0.05", 
"p < 0.05"), Text = c("To account for stimulus-and participant-level dependencies, we fitted crossed linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) and validated them with ordinal models across 171 candidate pairs, identifying nine predictor-emotion associations (Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate [FDR]-adjusted p < 0.05) involving six acoustic and spatial descriptors across six emotional dimensions.", 
"No GEMS dimension differed by formal musical training (all FDR-adjusted p = 1.000) or by sex (all FDR-adjusted p ≥ 0.212).", 
"After Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction, nine models showed significant fixed effects (adjusted p < 0.05; Table 1, Fig. 5) across six emotional dimensions.", 
"Note:The table details the 11 acoustic-emotional pairs that reached statistical significance following Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction (p < 0.05, across all 171 tests) under ordinal CLMM with a logit link function, using stimulus-level Student's t inference (df = 32) consistent with the primary linear LMMs."
)), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = 0.09 ", "p = 0.50", "p = 1.000", "p ≥ 0.212"), Sentence = c("Sex and musical training did not differ significantly across survey versions (exact Fisher-Freeman-Halton tests, p = 0.09 and p = 0.50), whereas age did (Kruskal-Wallis H = 16.93, p < 0.001; median age 25, 19, and 23 years in versions 1-3); its effect on mean ratings is absorbed by the survey-version covariate.", "Sex and musical training did not differ significantly across survey versions (exact Fisher-Freeman-Halton tests, p = 0.09 and p = 0.50), whereas age did (Kruskal-Wallis H = 16.93, p < 0.001; median age 25, 19, and 23 years in versions 1-3); its effect on mean ratings is absorbed by the survey-version covariate.", "No GEMS dimension differed by formal musical training (all FDR-adjusted p = 1.000) or by sex (all FDR-adjusted p ≥ 0.212).", "No GEMS dimension differed by formal musical training (all FDR-adjusted p = 1.000) or by sex (all FDR-adjusted p ≥ 0.212)." )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 3219 columns across 7 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 7 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: This study was conducted in accordance with the guidelines of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Ethics Committee of Universidad de Sevilla (Protocol code: SICEIA 2025-0156/ Date of approval: 25/06/2025).
live_data_statements: Participants were instructed to use headphones, set a comfortable listening volume, and listen in a quiet environment.

Participants were recruited by convenience sampling through university networks and social media, yielding 16, 18, and 34 completed sessions for the three versions (total N = 68 sessions from 65 participants).

The 13 baseline-only trials (1.6%) were spread across 8 sessions, and no participant gave baseline-only responses throughout a session (maximum 3 of 12 excerpts; individual means ≥ 1.21; peak ratings of 3-5), which suggests that low ratings reflected stimulus-specific neutrality rather than inattention.

Although participants were instructed to use headphones, we could not control the listening environment, the headphones used (whose frequency response differs between models), or the playback level, which adds unmodeled auditory variance.

info.title: GEMScapes: linking acoustic features to aesthetic emotions in ambient and cinematic music using the GEMS-9 scale

text.text: Ambient and cinematic music are widely used in behavioral and immersive multimedia paradigms, yet standardized stimulus sets with computational acoustic norms remain scarce.
We introduce GEMScapes, an open-access dataset of 38 original, high-fidelity instrumental tracks designed to elicit aesthetic emotions free from familiarity or semantic bias.

We combined computational acoustic profiling across temporal, spectral, cepstral, tonal, harmonic-percussive, rhythmic, and stereo spatial domains with 816 trial-level ratings of 36 of the tracks, provided by 65 participants in 68 listening sessions on the Geneva Emotional Music Scale (GEMS-9).

To account for stimulus-and participant-level dependencies, we fitted crossed linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) and validated them with ordinal models across 171 candidate pairs, identifying nine predictor-emotion associations (Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate [FDR]-adjusted p < 0.05) involving six acoustic and spatial descriptors across six emotional dimensions.
text.formatted: To account for stimulus-and participant-level dependencies, we fitted crossed linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) and validated them with ordinal models across 171 candidate pairs, identifying nine predictor-emotion associations (Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate [FDR]-adjusted p < 0.05) involving six acoustic and spatial descriptors across six emotional dimensions.

text.text: Temporal variability and soundstage spatialization were the main predictors: variability of spectral tilt predicted Tension, variability of percussive energy predicted Joyful Activation, Transcendence was associated with wider stereo width and smoother, non-percussive onsets, Peacefulness and Nostalgia with spectral stability, and Sadness with lower spectral brightness and reduced timbral modulation.
Variance partitioning revealed a continuum from strongly stimulus-driven states (Tension: 46% stimulus vs. 9% listener variance) to predominantly listener-dependent ones (Wonder: 8% vs.
GEMScapes provides an acoustically characterized resource for music perception, affective computing, and neurocognitive research.
Ambient and cinematic music is widely used to modulate affective and psychological states in multimedia production, immersive digital environments, and clinical interventions.

Despite this ubiquity, computational modeling of these structurally fluid genres remains underrepresented in Music Information Retrieval (MIR) and affective computing, where feature engineering and benchmark datasets have historically prioritized beat-driven popular genres (Panda et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Despite this ubiquity, computational modeling of these structurally fluid genres remains underrepresented in Music Information Retrieval (MIR) and affective computing, where feature engineering and benchmark datasets have historically prioritized beat-driven popular genres <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Panda et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Unlike much mainstream repertoire, ambient and cinematic compositions often dispense with vocals and rigid rhythmic grids, evoking emotion through subtle timbral evolution, sustained textures, and continuous dynamic contours.

Standard MIR taxonomies that collapse instrumental soundscapes into broad categories such as "electronic" or "classical" therefore obscure these dynamics, failing to capture gradual spectral morphing, low-frequency envelopes, and non-percussive temporal trajectories.

The Emotion-to-Music Mapping Atlas (EMMA; Strauss et al., 2024) is the main reference database of music excerpts rated with the Geneva Emotional Music Scale (GEMS; Jacobsen et al., 2025; Zentner et al., 2008).
text.formatted: The Emotion-to-Music Mapping Atlas (EMMA; <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Strauss et al., 2024)</ref> is the main reference database of music excerpts rated with the Geneva Emotional Music Scale (GEMS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Jacobsen et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Zentner et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: By targeting music-specific aesthetic affect rather than general core affect, the GEMS framework goes beyond traditional dimensional models such as Russell's (1980) valence-arousal space and captures nuanced emotional qualities uniquely elicited by musical engagement.
text.formatted: By targeting music-specific aesthetic affect rather than general core affect, the GEMS framework goes beyond traditional dimensional models such as <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Russell's (1980)</ref> valence-arousal space and captures nuanced emotional qualities uniquely elicited by musical engagement.

text.text: However, the original EMMA release includes only classical, pop, and hip-hop/rap excerpts.

Later additions include a subgenre labeled "ambient", but it consists mainly of vocal songs by popular artists (e.g., Björk, Imogen Heap, Moby) rather than instrumental, non-metric soundscapes such as those in GEMScapes, and there is no category for cinematic music.
Beyond their affective character, atmospheric soundscapes may also be useful for studying introspective, low-arousal states.

The Default Mode Network (DMN) supports internally directed attention and spontaneous thought (Buckner & DiNicola, 2019; Menon, 2023), and music listening has been linked to mind-wandering and to changes in DMN activity and connectivity (Taruffi et al., 2017; Wilkins et al., 2014).
text.formatted: The Default Mode Network (DMN) supports internally directed attention and spontaneous thought <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Buckner & DiNicola, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Menon, 2023)</ref>, and music listening has been linked to mind-wandering and to changes in DMN activity and connectivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Taruffi et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Wilkins et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: This possibility motivates our work combining ambient music with Virtual Reality (VR) to induce emotional states (Benítez et al., 2026; Fondón & Montesinos, 2025), with the longer-term aim of modulating DMN activity in immersive and clinical settings.
text.formatted: This possibility motivates our work combining ambient music with Virtual Reality (VR) to induce emotional states <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Benítez et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Fondón & Montesinos, 2025)</ref>, with the longer-term aim of modulating DMN activity in immersive and clinical settings.

text.text: Such applications require calibrated, standardized auditory stimuli with known acoustic properties and normative behavioral data.
To establish this baseline, we introduce GEMScapes, an open-access stimulus set of 38 high-fidelity instrumental tracks designed for affective and psychoacoustic research.
All tracks are original compositions produced with modular analog and digital synthesizers, avoiding commercial repertoire.
Recent psychometric evaluations indicate that musical familiarity is a major confound for emotional intensity (Jacobsen et al., 2025; Strauss et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Recent psychometric evaluations indicate that musical familiarity is a major confound for emotional intensity <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Jacobsen et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Strauss et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: By presenting completely novel stimuli, GEMScapes minimizes episodic memory retrieval and autobiographical associations (Juslin, 2013), favoring stimulusdriven affective responses.
text.formatted: By presenting completely novel stimuli, GEMScapes minimizes episodic memory retrieval and autobiographical associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Juslin, 2013)</ref>, favoring stimulusdriven affective responses.

text.text: Moreover, whereas widely used MIR and music-tagging datasets (e.g., Bogdanov et al., 2019; Defferrard et al., 2017) rely largely on vocal, metrically regular popular music, GEMScapes is exclusively instrumental and temporally flexible, which removes linguistic-semantic confounds and limits motor entrainment to a beat, supporting a tightly controlled stimulus set.
text.formatted: Moreover, whereas widely used MIR and music-tagging datasets (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bogdanov et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Defferrard et al., 2017)</ref> rely largely on vocal, metrically regular popular music, GEMScapes is exclusively instrumental and temporally flexible, which removes linguistic-semantic confounds and limits motor entrainment to a beat, supporting a tightly controlled stimulus set.

text.text: We extracted multi-domain acoustic and spatial descriptors (McFee et al., 2015) that preserve the native two-channel soundstage across temporal, rhythmic, spectral, cepstral, tonal, harmonic-percussive (HPSS), and stereo spatial dimensions.
text.formatted: We extracted multi-domain acoustic and spatial descriptors <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(McFee et al., 2015)</ref> that preserve the native two-channel soundstage across temporal, rhythmic, spectral, cepstral, tonal, harmonic-percussive (HPSS), and stereo spatial dimensions.

text.text: To link physical properties with subjective perception, we collected GEMS-9 ratings from participants for a subset of 36 tracks.
Using crossed linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) and variance partitioning, we separate stimulus-driven psychoacoustic predictors from listener-specific variance for each aesthetic emotion.
The complete dataset, including uncompressed audio files, the computational feature matrix, and trial-level behavioral ratings, is available on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21263434).
text.formatted: The complete dataset, including uncompressed audio files, the computational feature matrix, and trial-level behavioral ratings, is available on Zenodo (<ref type="url" target="https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21263434">https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21263434</ref>).

text.text: The reproducible statistical modeling code and analysis scripts are available in a companion Zenodo repository (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23216344).
text.formatted: The reproducible statistical modeling code and analysis scripts are available in a companion Zenodo repository (<ref type="url" target="https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23216344">https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23216344</ref>).

text.text: >Methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Methods</head>

text.text: The GEMScapes dataset comprises 38 original instrumental tracks (#001 to #038) composed and produced by the corresponding author.
The dataset combines pre-existing compositions from the author's repertoire with pieces created specifically for this study, sampling varied affective qualities across the atmospheric spectrum.
All tracks belong to the ambient and cinematic genres and feature long-attack synthesizer pads, evolving textures, and orchestral-style arrangements, without vocals.
To standardize exposure across computational and behavioral evaluations, each track was edited to a uniform duration of 60 s.
Master files were rendered as uncompressed stereo WAV files (48 kHz, 16-bit PCM).

Native two-channel stereo was preserved throughout the primary featureextraction and affective-modeling pipelines to retain soundstage spatialization and interchannel phase dynamics, and to avoid the phase cancellation that a mono downmix produces in wide ambient pads.
A companion feature set computed from the mono downmix is also provided in the dataset repository.
MIR feature extraction used a custom Python pipeline (available in the Zenodo repository, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21263434) built on librosa (McFee et al., 2015) and SciPy.
text.formatted: MIR feature extraction used a custom Python pipeline (available in the Zenodo repository, <ref type="url" target="https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21263434">https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21263434</ref>) built on librosa <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(McFee et al., 2015)</ref> and SciPy.

text.text: Time-frequency representations were computed with a short-time Fourier transform (STFT) using a 2,048-sample Hann window (≈42.7 ms at 48 kHz) and a hop size of 512 samples (≈10.7 ms; 75% overlap).
A feature space of 1,457 descriptors (1,459 columns, including file name and duration) was extracted across temporal, spectral, cepstral, tonal, rhythmic, HPSS, and stereo spatial domains.
Complete mathematical formulations, descriptive statistics, and per-track diagnostic figures are available in the repository.
Rather than relying on default MIR parameters optimized for beat-driven commercial music, the pipeline incorporated five adaptations to the characteristics of the recordings.
Continuous rhythmic representations.
Conventional tempo-estimation models assume an isochronous metrical grid and yield spurious estimates for non-pulsed textures.

Discrete beat tracking was therefore excluded, and temporal dynamics were described with continuous representations: summary statistics of the onset strength envelope, duration-normalized energy entropy, and autocorrelation and Fourier tempograms computed over a 768-frame window (≈8.19 s) and restricted to 15-240 BPM; the autocorrelation tempogram resolves slow pulses down to ≈15 BPM with at least two cycles per window.
Rhythmic entropy was derived from the Fourier tempogram (Müller, 2021), whose bin spacing of ≈7.3 BPM yields 30 bins between 22 and 234 BPM within that range.
text.formatted: Rhythmic entropy was derived from the Fourier tempogram <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Müller, 2021)</ref>, whose bin spacing of ≈7.3 BPM yields 30 bins between 22 and 234 BPM within that range.

text.text: To prevent transient noise from distorting tonal representations, median-filtering HPSS (kernel of 31 frames, ≈331 ms, by 31 bins, ≈727 Hz) separated stationary tonal components from broadband stochastic textures (e.g., granular synth textures, dynamic filter sweeps, and attack transients).
The CQT-based chromagrams, Tonnetz, and key profiles were computed on the harmonic layer (the STFT-based chromagram used the full signal).

Because a 48 kHz sampling rate implies a 24 kHz Nyquist frequency, all STFT-based spectral descriptors and the 128-band Mel filterbank (and the derived Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients, MFCCs) were restricted to the audible range (up to 20,000 Hz), so that inaudible ultrasonic content would not bias timbral metrics such as spectral contrast, flatness, and cepstral coefficients.
Native stereo.
Rather than downmixing to mono, the pipeline preserved the twochannel signal and extracted spatial descriptors such as stereo width and left-right (inter-channel) correlation.

An energy gate (-60 dBFS) excluded near-silent lead-ins and fadeout tails from the frame-level summary statistics of timbral, tonal, spatial, onset, and spectral-flux descriptors (level descriptors such as RMS used all frames), so that low-level noise floors would not bias dispersion metrics.

To limit multicollinearity in downstream modeling, we selected 19 low-redundancy acoustic and spatial descriptors that sample all extracted domains and were standardized (z-scores across the 38 tracks).

The subset showed moderate collinearity: the 19 × 19 Pearson correlation matrix yielded an eigenvalue condition number of κ = 90.8 (λmax / λmin), corresponding to a singular-value condition index of 9.53 for the standardized track-level data matrix (38 tracks by 19 features), below the conventional threshold of 30; only one feature pair exhibited |r| ≥ 0.70 (spectral centroid mean vs.
SD, r = 0.782), and these two descriptors also had the largest variance inflation factors (VIF = 14.7 and 7.5; ≤ 5.4 for all other descriptors).
Over the 36 rated tracks used in the mixed models, κ = 95.4 and the maximum VIF was 14.8.
The 19 descriptors sample seven domains: ( 1
text.formatted: The 19 descriptors sample seven domains: ( <ref type="formula">1</ref>

text.text: Affective ratings were collected through an online survey on Microsoft Forms.
Of the 38 tracks, 36 were evaluated across three independent survey versions (tracks #022 and #030 were withheld a priori to obtain three balanced 12-track blocks).
Because of platform constraints, the presentation order was fixed within each survey version.
To limit fatigue and carry-over effects, each participant rated 12 excerpts in a self-paced session (mean duration = 16.9 min, SD = 11.1).
All evaluations were completed remotely at the participants' homes, asynchronously and unsupervised.
Participants were instructed to use headphones, set a comfortable listening volume, and listen in a quiet environment.

Participants were recruited by convenience sampling through university networks and social media, yielding 16, 18, and 34 completed sessions for the three versions (total N = 68 sessions from 65 participants).
These sizes (16-34 raters per track) are consistent with those of comparable music-emotion studies (e.g., Strauss et al., 2024).
text.formatted: These sizes (16-34 raters per track) are consistent with those of comparable music-emotion studies (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Strauss et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Participants entered a pseudonymous code linked to personal data collected with informed consent (required in version 3 and optional in versions 1 and 2), which allowed the authors to identify three participants who took part in two versions (one in versions 1 and 2, and two in versions 2 and 3); because the versions comprise disjoint sets of tracks, they rated 24 different tracks and none of their ratings are repeated measurements of the same excerpt.
Each completed session (N = 68) was treated as one participant with its own random intercept.

Because each version was completed by a different sample and comprised a different set of tracks, survey version was included as a fixed covariate in all models, absorbing between-version differences in mean ratings regardless of their source.

Assigning a single identifier to each of the three participants who completed two versions (65 participants, all 816 ratings) left the same nine associations significant after FDR correction (|Δβ₁| ≤ 0.0002) and changed the variance shares by at most 1.1 percentage points (see the companion analytical repository).

Of the 65 participants, 55 (84.6%) provided demographic data; ages ranged from 18 to 63 years (M = 24.71, SD = 9.03; Mdn = 23.0, IQR = 3.50); 35 were male (63.6%) and 20 female (36.4%), and 17 reported significant formal musical training (30.9%) and 38 did not (69.1%).
Each participant was counted once in these summaries and in the betweenversion comparisons below, with the three participants who completed two versions assigned to the later version they completed.

Sex and musical training did not differ significantly across survey versions (exact Fisher-Freeman-Halton tests, p = 0.09 and p = 0.50), whereas age did (Kruskal-Wallis H = 16.93, p < 0.001; median age 25, 19, and 23 years in versions 1-3); its effect on mean ratings is absorbed by the survey-version covariate.
text.formatted: Sex and musical training did not differ significantly across survey versions (exact Fisher-Freeman-Halton tests, p = 0.09 and p = 0.50), whereas age did (Kruskal-Wallis H = 16.93, p < 0.001; median age 25, 19, and 23 years in versions 1-3); its effect on mean ratings is absorbed by the survey-version covariate.

text.text: Emotional responses were measured with the GEMS-9, a validated nine-dimension instrument optimized for music-induced affect (Jacobsen et al., 2025; Zentner et al., 2008;  used with the authorization of the original authors).
text.formatted: Emotional responses were measured with the GEMS-9, a validated nine-dimension instrument optimized for music-induced affect <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Jacobsen et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Zentner et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> used with the authorization of the original authors).

text.text: It covers nine aesthetic dimensions: Wonder, Transcendence, Power, Tenderness, Nostalgia, Peacefulness, Joyful Activation, Sadness, and Tension.
Emotional intensity was rated on a 5-point Likert scale: 1 ("not at all"), 2 ("a little"), 3 ("moderately"), 4 ("quite a bit"), and 5 ("very much").

To avoid fatigue across 108 ratings per session (12 tracks × 9 categories) and to discourage straight-lining, we used a selective-endorsement protocol: participants could leave blank the emotions they did not experience, and blank categories were recorded as the baseline value (1, "not at all"); in practice, only 239 of the 7,344 category ratings (3.3%) were left blank, and the remaining baseline values were explicit "not at all" responses.
Participants endorsed at least one emotion above baseline (rating ≥ 2) in 98.4% of trials (803 of 816).

The 13 baseline-only trials (1.6%) were spread across 8 sessions, and no participant gave baseline-only responses throughout a session (maximum 3 of 12 excerpts; individual means ≥ 1.21; peak ratings of 3-5), which suggests that low ratings reflected stimulus-specific neutrality rather than inattention.

Although responses concentrate at baseline (45.5% of all 7,344 individual category ratings; up to 65.9% for Tenderness), we assessed potential distortions from unequal category spacing and floor effects with crossed ordinal Cumulative Link Mixed Models (CLMMs; Section 2.5).
Each listening session covered the 12 tracks of one survey version, so the 816 ratings (68 sessions from 65 participants, 36 tracks) are grouped in two crossed ways: by participant and by track.
Ratings from the same participant share that person's scale use and baseline bias, and ratings of the same track share acoustic attributes that the predictor does not capture.

Standard linear regression and common machine-learning models treat observations as independent; ignoring this double clustering inflates Type I error and confounds stimulus-driven effects with listener response bias (Judd et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Standard linear regression and common machine-learning models treat observations as independent; ignoring this double clustering inflates Type I error and confounds stimulus-driven effects with listener response bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Judd et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: We therefore fitted crossed LMMs (Baayen et al., 2008), which model participant and track variability explicitly.
text.formatted: We therefore fitted crossed LMMs <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Baayen et al., 2008)</ref>, which model participant and track variability explicitly.

text.text: Rather than fitting a single saturated multivariate model, which would over-parameterize the stimulus space relative to the number of tracks (N = 36), inflate variance (multicollinearity), and obscure individual psychoacoustic relationships, we evaluated each of the 19 curated descriptors in a separate marginal LMM for each of the 9 GEMS dimensions (19 ×9 = 171 models).
Acoustic predictors were re-standardized (z-scores, M = 0, SD = 1) across the 36 evaluated tracks before model fitting, whereas ratings remained on their original 1-5 scale.
The fixed-effect slope β₁ therefore represents the expected change in Likert rating per +1 SD in the descriptor, which allows effect sizes to be compared across physical units.
On unaggregated trial-level data (N = 816), each model was specified as: where: • 𝑌 𝑖𝑗𝑘 is the Likert rating (1-5) assigned by participant 𝑖to musical excerpt 𝑗in survey version 𝑘.
• 𝛽 0 is the global fixed intercept.
• 𝑋 𝑗 is the standardized acoustic descriptor for excerpt 𝑗, with 𝛽 1 denoting the fixedeffect slope of interest.
• 𝑉 𝑖𝑗𝑘 is the dummy-coded categorical covariate controlling for survey version (Version 1 serving as reference).
• 𝑢 𝑖 part ∼ 𝒩(0, 𝜎 partfoot_0 ) is the random intercept for participant 𝑖, capturing individual baseline calibration and response bias.
text.formatted: • 𝑢 𝑖 part ∼ 𝒩(0, 𝜎 part<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> ) is the random intercept for participant 𝑖, capturing individual baseline calibration and response bias.

text.text: • 𝑤 𝑗 track ∼ 𝒩(0, 𝜎 track 2 ) is the crossed random intercept for musical track 𝑗, accounting for stimulus-specific variance beyond 𝑋 𝑗.
• 𝜀 𝑖𝑗𝑘 ∼ 𝒩(0, 𝜎 𝜀 2 ) is the residual error (combining participant x track interaction and measurement noise).
Models were fitted by restricted maximum likelihood (REML).

Because acoustic features vary across tracks (N = 36) and not across individual trials, tests of β₁ used Student's t distribution with conservative track-level degrees of freedom (𝑑𝑓 = 𝑁 tracks -𝑝 fixed = 36 -4 = 32; intercept, β₁, and two survey-version parameters), which avoids the anticonservative bias of asymptotic normal approximations.
Multiple testing across the 171 models was controlled with the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure at 0.05.
Sensitivity analyses of alternative degrees of freedom and randomslope structures are described in Section 2.5.

To quantify the relative contributions of acoustic stimuli and listener bias, we partitioned variance using null models, which keep survey version and the crossed random intercepts but omit the acoustic predictor.

For each GEMS dimension, total rating variance was decomposed into stimulus consensus (track intraclass correlation coefficient, ICC track = survey version was entered as a fixed effect, these shares are conditional on survey version (the variance it explains is not included in the denominator).

Approximate twosided 95% confidence intervals were obtained with a two-way cluster bootstrap that resampled tracks and participants with replacement within survey versions (B = 1,000 iterations per dimension; 9,000 fits in total).
Because dual-factor resampling alters cell structures, the replicate distributions were bias-corrected (shifted so that replicate means matched the point estimates) and clipped to [0, 1].

To verify that the primary trial-level LMM inferences were robust to data aggregation, response-scale discretization, degrees-of-freedom approximations, and random-effects structure, we ran three complementary analyses.
Track-level consensus.
Consensus ratings were computed as the arithmetic mean of participant scores for each of the 36 evaluated tracks.
Pearson correlations (r) were computed between each of the 19 standardized descriptors and each of the nine GEMS dimensions (171 pairs), with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control (0.05).

This analysis tests whether stimulus-level profiles converge with the trial-level LMMs when listener variance is averaged out, and it allows direct comparison with MIR studies that rely on aggregated stimulus norms (e.g., Strauss et al., 2024; Zentner et al., 2008).
text.formatted: This analysis tests whether stimulus-level profiles converge with the trial-level LMMs when listener variance is averaged out, and it allows direct comparison with MIR studies that rely on aggregated stimulus norms (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Strauss et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Zentner et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Because survey versions are confounded with the evaluated track subsets and cannot be entered as a covariate at the stimulus level, we additionally computed partial correlations after residualizing both acoustic and emotional variables on survey version (df = 32).
Ordinal modeling.

Because GEMS-9 ratings are discrete 5-point Likert responses, we tested whether treating them as continuous in linear LMMs introduced distortion from unequal category spacing or floor effects (baseline responses were 45% of ratings, 66% for Tenderness).

All 171 pairs were re-estimated with CLMMs (logit link) and the same crossed random-effects structure: logit[𝑃(𝑌 𝑖𝑗𝑘 ≤ 𝑐)] = 𝜃 𝑐 -(𝛽 1 𝑋 𝑗 + ∑ 𝛽 2,𝑘 3 𝑘=2 𝑉 𝑖𝑗𝑘 + 𝑢 𝑖 part + 𝑤 𝑗 track ) where θc are the threshold cut-points between response categories c ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4}, and the remaining terms mirror the primary crossed LMM specification (see Section 2.4).
Slopes were exponentiated to odds ratios (OR = exp(β₁)), the multiplicative change in the odds of a higher rating per +1 SD in the descriptor.

Because Python statistical libraries do not support crossed-random-effects ordinal models, CLMMs were fitted in R with the clmm function of the ordinal package (maximum likelihood, Laplace approximation).

Inference used stimulus-level Student's t tests (df = 32), consistent with the primary LMMs, alongside asymptotic Wald z tests and likelihood-ratio tests for singular fits, with FDR control (0.05) across all 171 ordinal models.

text.text: Feature extraction across the 38 tracks yielded 1,457 acoustic and spatial descriptors per track (temporal, rhythmic, spectral, cepstral, tonal, harmonic-percussive, and spatial domains).
To avoid high-dimensional redundancy and to keep the psychoacoustic modeling interpretable, we evaluated a curated, low-redundancy subset of 19 descriptors.

The Pearson correlation matrix of these 19 descriptors (Fig. 1) showed broad independence across domains, with a few natural acoustic couplings: spectral centroid mean and SD (r = 0.782), Onset Strength SD and rhythmic entropy (r = -0.632), integrated loudness and percussive energy SD (r = 0.605), spectral centroid SD and MFCC 1 SD (r = 0.584), and stereo width and phase correlation SD (r = 0.565).

text.text: Across domains, all pairwise correlations were moderate (|r| < 0.65), and the feature space was acceptably conditioned (κ = 90.8; condition index = 9.5), with collinearity concentrated in the spectral centroid mean/SD pair (maximum VIF = 14.7).

text.text: Agglomerative hierarchical clustering with Ward's minimum-variance criterion on the 19 standardized descriptors partitioned the 38 tracks into three acoustic clusters (Fig. 2).
text.formatted: Agglomerative hierarchical clustering with Ward's minimum-variance criterion on the 19 standardized descriptors partitioned the 38 tracks into three acoustic clusters (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">2</ref>).

text.text: Cluster separation was weak (mean silhouette = 0.07 for k = 3; the highest value, 0.16, was obtained for k = 2), so the partition is used as a descriptive grouping of the tracks rather than as evidence of discrete acoustic types.

Cluster 1 (N = 7) grouped tracks with prominent attack transients (high Onset Strength SD and percussive energy SD) and brighter spectra (high spectral centroid mean and SD), together with lower harmonic dominance and narrower stereo width.
Cluster 2 (N = 17) comprised tracks dominated by sustained harmonic and tonal structure, with high harmonic dominance, pronounced spectral contrast, high key strength, and low chroma entropy.

Cluster 3 (N = 14) captured expansive ambient soundscapes defined by wide stereo width, high rhythmic entropy, and pronounced spatial modulation (high ILD SD and phase correlation SD), with attenuated attack transients and minimal percussive energy.
Descriptive statistics confirm the largely non-pulsed, textural acoustic profile of GEMScapes.
Temporally, the tracks had diffuse rhythmic structure.

Onset strength, which has no absolute scale, averaged 0.85 (SD = 0.19), with a mean within-track SD of 0.84 (SD = 0.62); rhythmic entropy, normalized to [0, 1] with 1 indicating that no tempo dominates, averaged 0.84 (SD = 0.12), which reflects evolving soundscapes rather than periodic metrical grids.

Dynamically, the tracks had a controlled energy profile, with a mean dynamic range of 13.72 dB (SD = 5.23 dB; difference between the 95th and 5th percentiles of RMS energy) and a mean integrated loudness of -16.40 LUFS (SD = 2.99 LUFS).
Spectrally, energy was concentrated in the low-to-mid registers (mean spectral centroid = 1,465 Hz, SD = 806 Hz).
Spatially, the tracks exhibited expansive soundstages

text.text: Individual tracks The original GEMS framework groups music-induced emotions into three second-order factors: Sublimity (Wonder, Transcendence, Tenderness, Nostalgia, Peacefulness), Vitality (Joyful Activation, Power), and Unease (Tension, Sadness) (Zentner et al., 2008).

text.text: Exploratory demographic comparisons in the subsample with demographic data (N = 55 participants) were performed at the participant level (median of each participant's 12 or 24 ratings per dimension; two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction across the nine dimensions).
No GEMS dimension differed by formal musical training (all FDR-adjusted p = 1.000) or by sex (all FDR-adjusted p ≥ 0.212).

Given the small subgroups (e.g., 17 participants with significant musical training), these null results should be interpreted with caution, and they do not imply the absence of listener-specific variability, which the variance partitioning below quantifies.

We first cross-referenced the unsupervised acoustic clusters (Fig. 2) with the dominant emotion of each track (the dimension with the highest median rating, ties broken by the mean rating; Supplemental Fig. S1), which showed alignment with arousal and soundstage spatialization.
text.formatted: We first cross-referenced the unsupervised acoustic clusters (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">2</ref>) with the dominant emotion of each track (the dimension with the highest median rating, ties broken by the mean rating; Supplemental Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_18">S1</ref>), which showed alignment with arousal and soundstage spatialization.

text.text: Cluster 1 (N = 7), defined by prominent attack transients and brighter spectra, contained mostly high-arousal, activating pieces: 5 of its 7 tracks had Joyful Activation (3 tracks) or Power (2 tracks) as the dominant emotion.
Contemplative, low-arousal states concentrated in the harmonically dominated tonal branch (Cluster 2, N = 17), where 11 of 17 tracks had a Sublimity dimension as the dominant emotion:
Transcendence (4 tracks), Nostalgia (4), Peacefulness (2), and Tenderness (1).

Cluster 3 (N = 14), the expansive ambient branch, spanned immersive soundscapes that alternated between serene contemplation (Peacefulness and Transcendence; 6 tracks) and dark atmospheric suspense (Tension; 3 tracks).
Because 16 of the 36 rated tracks tie on their highest median, these counts depend on the tie-breaking rule and should be read as indicative.
This loose correspondence between acoustic clusters and dominant emotions motivates trial-level mixed models to identify the continuous acoustic correlates of each emotion.
To identify these correlates, we evaluated the 19 curated descriptors against all nine GEMS dimensions (19 ×9 = 171 crossed LMMs).
After Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction, nine models showed significant fixed effects (adjusted p < 0.05; Table 1, Fig. 5) across six emotional dimensions.

text.text: Stimulus-driven variance exceeded listener variance in six of the nine dimensions and peaked for Tension (46.1% stimulus vs.
8.8% listener variance).
Transcendence (18.6% vs.
22.7%) marked the inflection point at which listener variance began to exceed stimulus variance.
At the other extreme, individual listener differences dominated Sadness (29.2% listener vs.
11.2% stimulus) and Wonder (31.7% vs.
8.0%), accounting for roughly 2.6 and 4 times more variance, respectively, than the music itself.
Residual variance ranged from 45.1% to 60.3%, reflecting single-trial measurement error and unmodeled participant × track interactions.
The three sensitivity analyses described in Section 2.5 gave results that converge with the primary LMMs.
Track-level consensus.
Mean ratings per track were correlated with all 19 descriptors across the 171 pairs (Supplemental Figs. S2 and S3) with FDR correction.

text.text: The analysis yielded nine significant associations (|r| = 0.50-0.65), which replicated all nine associations from the trial-level LMMs with identical signs and comparable relative magnitudes.
With survey version partialled out (df = 32), the same nine associations remained significant after FDR adjustment.

Unadjusted and partial correlation coefficients were virtually identical across the 171 pairs (r = 0.995; median absolute difference = 0.01), so macro-level stimulus norms converge with the trial-level mixedeffects results and the survey blocking design does not confound them.
Ordinal modeling.

Predictor signs and relative magnitudes in the CLMMs agreed closely with the linear LMM estimates: directional sign agreement was 98.8% (169 of 171 models), and the correlation between linear slopes (β₁) and ordinal log-odds (log OR) was r = 0.98.

All nine associations significant in the primary LMMs remained significant in the CLMMs under both conservative stimulus-level inference (Student's t, df = 32; 11 significant pairs in total; Supplemental Table S1) and asymptotic Wald z inference (17 pairs in total).
text.formatted: All nine associations significant in the primary LMMs remained significant in the CLMMs under both conservative stimulus-level inference (Student's t, df = 32; 11 significant pairs in total; Supplemental Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">S1</ref>) and asymptotic Wald z inference (17 pairs in total).

text.text: Under the df = 32 criterion, only two additional associations reached significance: Peacefulness was negatively predicted by Spectral Centroid Mean (OR = 0.48), and Sadness was positively predicted by HPSS Harmonic Dominance Mean (OR = 1.73).
Three models showed numerical non-convergence, none involving a significant predictor.
This close correspondence indicates that the main psychoacoustic findings are robust to response-scale discretization and floor effects.
Alternative LMM specifications.
Satterthwaite degrees of freedom (range 29.1-34.9, median 32.2) yielded the same nine significant associations after FDR correction.
Adding by-participant random slopes for each descriptor left all nine associations significant, with negligible changes in standard errors (median standard-error ratio = 1.01, maximum = 1.11).

With only 12 tracks per session, the data contain little information on how each participant's sensitivity to a descriptor differs from the average, and in 81 of the 171 models this random-slope variance could not be estimated reliably (singular fit).
This supports the simpler crossed random-intercept specification used in the primary analysis.
Full model outputs and diagnostics for all 171 specifications are in the companion analytical repository.
In this study, we related the acoustic features of 36 original ambient and cinematic tracks to the aesthetic emotions reported by listeners.
As these pieces lack lyrics and have little metric regularity, their emotional character is likely to be carried by timbre, dynamics, texture, and spatial image rather than by words or rhythm.
Six of the nine GEMS-9 dimensions showed consistent associations with specific acoustic descriptors.
Because the descriptors vary together across tracks rather than independently, and all tracks were written by a single composer, these results describe associations rather than causal effects.
The emotions also differed in how much listeners agreed on them (Table 2).
text.formatted: The emotions also differed in how much listeners agreed on them (Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: Agreement was highest for emotions at both ends of the arousal dimension, such as Tension and Joyful Activation on one side and Peacefulness and Tenderness on the other; for Tension, the track accounted for 46.1% of rating variance and the listener for only 8.8%.
At the other extreme, Sadness and Wonder varied mainly between listeners (for Wonder, 8.0% vs.
31.7%), which may reflect personal associations, mood, or individual use of the rating scale.
These emotions are therefore harder to target through the acoustic properties of a stimulus alone.
The co-occurrence of emotions across tracks (Fig. 4) only partly matched the original GEMS structure (Zentner et al., 2008).
text.formatted: The co-occurrence of emotions across tracks (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_9">4</ref>) only partly matched the original GEMS structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Zentner et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: The clearest departure was Sadness, which grouped with the contemplative emotions rather than with Tension; this fits the idea that sadness in music is often experienced as a calm, pleasurable melancholy rather than as real distress (Taruffi & Koelsch, 2014).

text.text: Wonder showed the opposite shift, correlating with Tension rather than with the calm emotions of the Sublimity factor.
Tension was associated with how much the spectrum changed over time rather than with its average character.

Its only significant predictor was the variability of spectral tilt (MFCC 1 SD; Table 1, Fig. 6), which reflects changes in the balance between low-and high-frequency energy and is related to fluctuations in brightness (r = 0.58 with Spectral Centroid SD; Fig. 1).

text.text: Brightness itself, indexed by the mean spectral centroid (Schubert, 2004), did not predict Tension: tracks #012 and #028, for example, were relatively bright (spectral centroid mean in the upper third of the dataset) but spectrally stable (MFCC 1 SD in the lowest fifth), and received minimal Tension ratings (Mdn = 1.0).

text.text: This pattern is compatible with accounts in which changing sounds capture attention and raise arousal.

Brainstem reflexes respond to sudden or changing acoustic events that may signal something important (Juslin, 2013), and unpredictable changes can violate auditory expectations (Huron, 2006), whereas a stable spectrum may allow listeners to habituate.
text.formatted: Brainstem reflexes respond to sudden or changing acoustic events that may signal something important <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Juslin, 2013)</ref>, and unpredictable changes can violate auditory expectations <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Huron, 2006)</ref>, whereas a stable spectrum may allow listeners to habituate.

text.text: Continuous variation in psychoacoustic features has also been linked to moment-tomoment changes in felt emotion (Coutinho & Cangelosi, 2011).
text.formatted: Continuous variation in psychoacoustic features has also been linked to moment-tomoment changes in felt emotion <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Coutinho & Cangelosi, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Because we collected no physiological data, these mechanisms remain hypotheses.
Joyful Activation was associated with a different kind of variability.

Its only significant predictor was the variability of percussive energy (HPSS percussive energy SD; Table 1, Fig. 6): tracks in which transient energy fluctuated more received higher Joyful Activation ratings.
text.formatted: Its only significant predictor was the variability of percussive energy (HPSS percussive energy SD; Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>, Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_11">6</ref>): tracks in which transient energy fluctuated more received higher Joyful Activation ratings.

text.text: This agrees with structural accounts in which acoustic energy and transient events are primary cues for activation in music (Gabrielsson & Lindström, 2010).
text.formatted: This agrees with structural accounts in which acoustic energy and transient events are primary cues for activation in music <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Gabrielsson & Lindström, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In beat-based music, such effects are often attributed to motor entrainment and its links with reward (Salimpoor et al., 2011; Vuilleumier & Trost, 2015).
text.formatted: In beat-based music, such effects are often attributed to motor entrainment and its links with reward <ref type="bibr">(Salimpoor et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Vuilleumier & Trost, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Our predictor, however, measures how much percussive energy varies, not whether it follows a regular pulse, so whether entrainment contributes to this association remains to be tested.
The more introspective emotions showed the opposite profile: less variability and, for Transcendence, a wider stereo image (Table 1, Fig. 6).
text.formatted: The more introspective emotions showed the opposite profile: less variability and, for Transcendence, a wider stereo image (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>, Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_11">6</ref>).

text.text: Transcendence was the only dimension associated with a spatial descriptor.

It increased with stereo width (Stereo Width Mean) and decreased with the variability of onset strength (Onset Strength SD), so it was rated higher for wide, enveloping textures without marked attacks.

Peacefulness and Nostalgia were associated with spectral stability: both decreased with fluctuations in brightness (Spectral Centroid SD), and Nostalgia also decreased with spectral-tilt variability (MFCC 1 SD).
One possible interpretation draws on predictive accounts of music perception, in which marked, regular events continuously engage prediction and motor preparation (Koelsch et al., 2019).
text.formatted: One possible interpretation draws on predictive accounts of music perception, in which marked, regular events continuously engage prediction and motor preparation <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Koelsch et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Smooth, stable textures offer few such anchors and may leave attention free to turn inward.

This would be consistent with evidence that low-arousal musical emotions such as Peacefulness, Nostalgia, and Sadness engage ventromedial prefrontal regions that overlap with the default network (Trost et al., 2012), and that music can promote mindwandering and change DMN centrality (Taruffi et al., 2017).

text.text: Wonder and Sadness, the two emotions that depended most on the listener, differed in their acoustic profiles.
Wonder had no significant predictor, consistent with its small stimulus share (8.0%; Table 2).
text.formatted: Wonder had no significant predictor, consistent with its small stimulus share (8.0%; Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: Sadness, in contrast, was associated with darker and more stable timbre (lower Spectral Centroid Mean and SD, two strongly correlated descriptors), although these were the smallest of the nine effects (|β₁| ≈ 0.2).
The ordinal models also linked Sadness to higher harmonic dominance (Section 3.4), but this association was not significant in the primary linear models.
Although Power showed substantial stimulus variance (24.5%; Table 2), no descriptor predicted it after FDR correction.
text.formatted: Although Power showed substantial stimulus variance (24.5%; Table <ref type="table">2</ref>), no descriptor predicted it after FDR correction.

text.text: The strongest non-significant candidates were a larger Tonnetz fifths radius, lower harmonic dominance, and lower upper-mid spectral contrast (Fig. 5).
text.formatted: The strongest non-significant candidates were a larger Tonnetz fifths radius, lower harmonic dominance, and lower upper-mid spectral contrast (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">5</ref>).

text.text: Lower harmonic dominance reached significance only in the ordinal models with asymptotic Wald inference, not with the conservative stimulus-level test (full results in the companion repository).
These trends point in a direction suggested by research on film music.

Traditional accounts link tonal expectation and harmonic resolution to positive valence and reduced anxiety (Huron, 2006; Margulis, 2005), whereas in modern cinematic scoring, impressions of vastness and power are often created by acoustic roughness, broadband textures, or ambiguous modal shifts that lower harmonic dominance (Lahdelma & Eerola, 2020; Lehman, 2018).

text.text: Because none of these associations reached significance in the primary models, this interpretation remains speculative and requires replication.
GEMScapes provides acoustically characterized stimuli with normative emotional ratings, together with an estimate of how much each emotion depends on the stimulus rather than on the listener.

For sound design, the associations reported here could serve as initial guidelines for adaptive audio and interactive soundscapes, particularly for emotions on which listeners agreed most, such as Tension and Peacefulness.

The association of a wide stereo image and smooth onsets with Transcendence, for example, suggests a starting point for spatial audio in immersive VR, pending replication with music by other composers and with other listener groups.

For experimental and clinical research, the acoustic profiles associated with Peacefulness and Transcendence (low attack variability, a stable spectral centroid, and a wide stereo image) offer reference points for selecting or designing stimuli, including for closed-loop, biofeedback-driven VR environments (Agres et al., 2021; Benítez et al., 2026).

text.text: Because the stimuli are described parametrically, future fMRI and EEG studies could vary these properties systematically and test whether they modulate DMN activity and connectivity, which can change with music listening (Wilkins et al., 2014).

text.text: Although the main results were robust to data aggregation, ordinal modeling, and alternative model specifications (Section 3.4), several limitations define their scope.
First, all 38 tracks were composed and produced by a single author.

This was an intentional choice to ensure consistent production and to avoid prior familiarity, but it also limits stylistic variety to one composer's musical vocabulary, so some associations may reflect specific sound-design habits rather than features of the genre as a whole.

The crossed random intercepts account for track-specific idiosyncrasies, but they cannot separate composer style from genre; replicating these analyses with ambient music by other composers is an important next step.
Second, ratings were collected online, at participants' homes and without supervision.

Although participants were instructed to use headphones, we could not control the listening environment, the headphones used (whose frequency response differs between models), or the playback level, which adds unmodeled auditory variance.
In addition, presentation order was fixed within each survey version, so order effects are confounded with track identity.

Listeners nevertheless showed no clear signs of fatigue: excerpts late in the sequence still received some of the highest ratings for contrasting emotions (e.g., Joyful Activation for track #032 at position 9, and Nostalgia for #009 and Tension for #027 at position 11; all Mdn = 4.0).
Laboratory replications with calibrated playback would help assess finer timbral effects.
Third, the sample was mainly composed of young adults (M age = 24.7 years, SD = 9.03, among the 55 participants with demographic data) without significant formal musical training (69.1%).
The results therefore describe non-expert listeners, and future studies should include older, musically trained, and cross-cultural groups.
Finally, because acoustic features vary only between tracks, the effective sample size for testing them is the 36 rated tracks rather than the 816 ratings.
Weaker associations may therefore have gone undetected; Tenderness, for example, showed substantial stimulus variance (Table 2) but no significant predictor.

text.text: Detecting such effects would require larger sets of stimuli.
The exploratory demographic comparisons were similarly limited by the small size of the subgroups.
GEMScapes provides 38 original ambient and cinematic tracks with acoustic descriptors and normative GEMS-9 ratings, openly available for research on music and emotion.

In these tracks, emotions were associated mainly with how the sound changes over time and how widely it spreads across the stereo field, and some emotions depended far more on the listener than on the music.
Both points are worth considering when selecting or designing auditory stimuli for affective and neurocognitive research.

The resulting structure is organized mainly by arousal.
A low-arousal introspective cluster emerged, with strong positive correlations among Peacefulness, Nostalgia, and Tenderness (Nostalgia-Peacefulness, ρ = 0.90; Nostalgia-Tenderness, ρ = 0.74).
Sadness, conventionally grouped under Unease, aligned with this soothing cluster (ρ = 0.64 with Peacefulness; ρ = 0.61 with Nostalgia).
Tension correlated negatively with the introspective group (Peacefulness, ρ = -0.77; Nostalgia, ρ = -0.77; Tenderness, ρ = -0.69).
Wonder diverged from the Sublimity cluster: it correlated negatively with Nostalgia (ρ = -0.64), Tenderness (ρ = -0.57), and Peacefulness (ρ = -0.51) and positively with Tension (ρ = 0.50).
Power and Transcendence were also positively correlated (ρ = 0.49), an association that crosses the original Vitality and Sublimity factors.
